items.prompt: Which of these is NOT the kind of thing this unit means by 'a secret'?
choices: A Stripe secret API key
The title of a public marketing blog post
A production database password
A webhook signing secret
items.explanation: A secret is something that, if read by someone outside its intended audience, lets them act as your system or read data they shouldn't — a public blog post's title is meant to be public, so there's nothing to protect. The other three all grant real capability (billing/data access, database read-write, forging trusted events) if leaked.
items.reference:
🔑 Secret

grants capability if leaked (API key, DB password, private key)

📰 Not a secret

meant to be public (blog title, marketing copy)

Why: the test isn't "does it look sensitive," it's "does having it let someone do something they shouldn't be able to do."

items.prompt: A team treats a webhook signing secret casually — pasted into a shared doc alongside non-sensitive config. What's the concrete risk if it leaks?
choices: None — webhook secrets are only used for logging
An attacker could forge webhook events your system trusts as genuine
It would only affect the webhook provider, never your own system
Webhook secrets rotate automatically, so leaking one is harmless
items.explanation: A webhook signing secret is how your system verifies an incoming event genuinely came from the provider (Stripe, GitHub, etc.) and wasn't forged. Leak it, and an attacker can craft a fake event — a fake 'payment succeeded' webhook, for instance — that your system will process as if it were real.
items.reference:
🔑 Secret

grants capability if leaked (API key, DB password, private key)

📰 Not a secret

meant to be public (blog title, marketing copy)

Why: the test isn't "does it look sensitive," it's "does having it let someone do something they shouldn't be able to do."

items.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches a leaked secret type to what it grants an attacker?
choices: SSH deploy key → ability to impersonate the server or push code as you
SSH deploy key → only lets someone read public repository names
Database credential → only affects billing, never data
Cloud provider access key → grants nothing without also having the AWS console password
items.explanation: An SSH deploy key is a credential that proves identity for git/server operations — leaking it lets an attacker push code as you or connect to a server as you. A cloud provider access key is independently usable (it doesn't require a separate console password) and grants exactly whatever IAM permissions it carries; a database credential grants direct data access, not just billing.

🔑 Secret

grants capability if leaked (API key, DB password, private key)

📰 Not a secret

meant to be public (blog title, marketing copy)

Why: the test isn't "does it look sensitive," it's "does having it let someone do something they shouldn't be able to do."

items.prompt: A CI build step runs `echo "Connecting with $DB_PASSWORD"` for debugging, and the CI system's build logs are readable by every engineer in the org. Which leak vector is this?
choices: Docker image layers
CI logs
Client-side bundles
Git history
items.explanation: This is the CI-log vector: a debug print writes the secret straight into log output that's often more widely readable than the source repository itself, and log retention windows (often 30-90+ days) mean it stays readable long after the build finishes.
items.reference:
📜
Git history
🖨️
CI logs
🩹
Error trackers
📦
Client bundles
🐳
Docker layers

Why: each vector is a normal workflow step that happens to copy a value somewhere nobody thought to check.

items.prompt: A Dockerfile `COPY`s a credentials file into an image, uses it during the build, then `RUN rm credentials.json` in a later layer. Is the secret actually gone from the final image?
choices: Yes — deleting the file in a later layer removes it from the image entirely
No — the earlier layer that copied it in is still part of the image and can be inspected
Only if the image was built with `--squash`, otherwise it depends on the base image
It depends only on whether the image is pushed to a public or private registry
items.explanation: Docker images are layered — each instruction creates a new layer on top of the previous one, and a later layer's deletion doesn't remove data from an earlier layer, it just hides it from the final filesystem view. Anyone who can pull the image can inspect every layer, including the one where the credentials file briefly existed.

items.prompt: A frontend app reads `process.env.INTERNAL_API_SECRET` and bundles it into the JavaScript served to every visitor's browser, reasoning 'it's still environment-variable injection, so it's fine.' What's wrong with this?
choices: Nothing — environment-variable injection is always safe regardless of where the code runs
The value is baked into client-side code at build time, so every visitor's browser receives it — it was never actually secret
It's only a problem if the site doesn't use HTTPS
It's fine as long as the variable name doesn't contain the word 'secret'
items.explanation: Env-var injection protects a value from being committed to source — it says nothing about where the resulting code runs. Anything baked into frontend JavaScript at build time ships to every visitor who loads the page; 'it came from an environment variable' doesn't change that the value is now publicly readable in the browser's dev tools.

items.prompt: Mira deletes the hardcoded password line and commits the fix 47 minutes after the original push. Is the incident over at that point?
choices: Yes — the current file no longer contains the password
No — the password was live and usable for 47 minutes, and deleting a line doesn't invalidate the value itself
Yes, as long as the repository is also made private again
No, but only because the repo was accidentally public — a private repo leak wouldn't need rotation
items.explanation: Deleting the line stops the file from showing the secret going forward, but it does nothing to the value itself — the actual database still accepts that password until someone changes it. The only action that ends the exposure is rotation (changing the value at the system that accepts it), regardless of repo visibility.
items.reference:
🗑️ Delete the file

hides the value going forward — the old value still works

🔄 Rotate the value

the only action that actually ends the exposure

Why: a secret's exposure ends when the value stops being accepted, not when a file stops showing it.

items.prompt: A team adds `.env` to `.gitignore` after discovering it had been committed with real secrets inside. They consider the matter closed. What's missing?
choices: Nothing — `.gitignore` prevents the file from being committed again
The secrets that were already committed are still valid and still in git history — they still need to be rotated
`.gitignore` should be applied to the whole repository, not just `.env`, or it won't work at all
This is only a problem for public repositories
items.explanation: `.gitignore` is forward-looking — it stops the file from being committed again, but every secret value that was already committed is unaffected: it's still sitting in git history, still valid, and still exactly as usable by anyone who already has (or later gets) a copy of that history. Preventing a future mistake and undoing a past exposure are two different problems.
items.reference:
🗑️ Delete the file

hides the value going forward — the old value still works

🔄 Rotate the value

the only action that actually ends the exposure

Why: a secret's exposure ends when the value stops being accepted, not when a file stops showing it.

items.prompt: Mira reasons 'it's just a temporary branch, I'll fix it before merging, so hardcoding is fine for now.' What actually makes this reasoning fail?
choices: Nothing — temporary branches are never seen by anyone until merged
A push to any branch is already committed to history and can already be cloned, scanned, or forked, regardless of merge status
It only fails if the branch is later deleted without merging
Branches are safe as long as they don't have 'temp' or 'wip' in the name
items.explanation: 'Temporary' describes intent, not what git actually does — the moment a commit is pushed, it exists in the remote's history and is reachable by anyone with clone access (or a scanning bot), whether or not that branch is ever merged. The fix has to happen before the push, not before the merge.
items.reference:
❌ Hardcoded

value lives in source — committed, cloned, scanned

✅ Env-var injected

source only holds a reference — nothing to leak from the repo itself

Why: the risk is created the moment the value enters source control, not at merge time.

items.prompt: What's the core difference between a hardcoded secret and one supplied via environment-variable injection?
choices: Environment variables are automatically encrypted, hardcoded values are not
Source code holds a reference (a variable name) instead of the literal value, so there's nothing secret to leak from the repo itself
There's no real difference — both end up in the running process's memory the same way
Environment variables can only be used for numbers, not passwords
items.explanation: Both approaches result in the value being available to the running process — that part is identical. The difference is entirely about what's in source control: a hardcoded value is committed and lives in history forever; an injected value's source code contains only a reference, so a git leak, a code review, or a public repo never exposes the actual secret.
items.reference:
❌ Hardcoded

value lives in source — committed, cloned, scanned

✅ Env-var injected

source only holds a reference — nothing to leak from the repo itself

Why: the risk is created the moment the value enters source control, not at merge time.

items.prompt: One shared admin database credential is used by every microservice in a company. If a single service's credential leaks, what's the blast radius?
choices: Only that one service's data
Every table across every service, since it's the same shared admin credential
Nothing — leaking a credential from one service doesn't affect others
Only read access, never write access
items.explanation: A shared credential means every consumer's leak is equivalent to leaking the most powerful version of that credential — since it's the same admin credential everywhere, a leak from the least-important service grants exactly as much access as a leak from the most sensitive one.
items.reference:
ScopingBlast radius if leaked
One shared admin credentialEvery table, every service
Per-service credentialOnly that service's data
Per-service, per-environmentStaging leak can't touch production

Why: scoping bounds what one leak can reach, independent of whether the leak happens at all.

items.prompt: A staging environment and a production environment share the exact same database credential 'to keep things simple.' What's the specific risk this creates?
choices: None — staging and production data are usually similar anyway
A leaked staging credential (often less carefully guarded) can be used to reach production directly
This only matters if staging and production run on different cloud providers
Shared credentials make rotation easier, so this is a net safety improvement
items.explanation: Staging environments are typically treated with less caution — more people have access, logging is more permissive, testing tools poke at it more freely — which makes a staging leak more likely, not less. Sharing the credential means that more-likely leak grants the same access as a production leak would.
items.reference:
ScopingBlast radius if leaked
One shared admin credentialEvery table, every service
Per-service credentialOnly that service's data
Per-service, per-environmentStaging leak can't touch production

Why: scoping bounds what one leak can reach, independent of whether the leak happens at all.

items.prompt: Why does a secret manager make least-privilege scoping (many narrow credentials instead of one broad one) actually practical, rather than just theoretically nice?
choices: It doesn't — narrow scoping is equally easy to maintain by hand regardless of tooling
It centralizes minting, storing, and rotating many credentials, which is a maintenance burden no team keeps up with by hand
Secret managers automatically merge all credentials into one for convenience
Least-privilege scoping is only relevant for encryption keys, not application credentials
items.explanation: Twelve narrow, well-scoped credentials are more secure in principle than one broad one, but only if someone actually creates and rotates all twelve — a task teams reliably abandon when it's manual. A secret manager makes minting and rotating many credentials routine instead of a maintenance burden, which is what turns the theory into something teams actually do.
items.reference:
ScopingBlast radius if leaked
One shared admin credentialEvery table, every service
Per-service credentialOnly that service's data
Per-service, per-environmentStaging leak can't touch production

Why: scoping bounds what one leak can reach, independent of whether the leak happens at all.

items.prompt: A secret is added in commit A and deleted in commit B. Running `git log -p --all` on the repository at HEAD (after commit B) — what does it show for commit A's diff?
choices: Nothing — commit B's deletion also removes commit A's diff from history
Commit A's full diff, including the secret, exactly as it was originally committed
Only a redacted version showing that a secret existed, not the value itself
It depends on whether commit B was a merge commit or a direct commit
items.explanation: Git is a history of changes, not a single mutable file — commit B adds a new state on top of commit A, it doesn't rewrite or erase it. `git log -p` walks every commit in the requested range and shows each one's diff exactly as recorded, so commit A's addition of the secret is fully visible forever unless history is explicitly rewritten.
items.reference:
commit A: password added → commit B: password deleted
both commits still exist — B doesn't erase A, it adds on top of it

Why: "the file looks clean at HEAD" and "the repository is clean" are different claims — only scanning full history checks the second one.

items.prompt: Between commit A (secret added) and commit B (secret removed), three teammates cloned the repository and a CI runner cached a checkout. After commit B is pushed, are those three clones and the CI cache affected?
choices: Yes — pushing commit B automatically updates every existing clone
No — each of those clones and the cache already has commit A's full history on disk, unaffected by anything pushed afterward to the original remote
Only the CI cache is affected, since it re-syncs automatically before every build
It depends on whether the teammates later run `git pull`
items.explanation: A clone or a CI checkout is an independent copy of the repository's history at the moment it was made — pushing new commits to the original remote doesn't reach into copies that already exist elsewhere. Even running `git pull` later would only add commit B on top; it wouldn't remove commit A from the local history that clone already has.
items.reference:
commit A: password added → commit B: password deleted
both commits still exist — B doesn't erase A, it adds on top of it

Why: "the file looks clean at HEAD" and "the repository is clean" are different claims — only scanning full history checks the second one.

items.prompt: A team force-pushes a rewritten history that removes a leaked secret from every commit in the canonical repository. Does this, by itself, end the exposure?
choices: Yes — force-pushing a rewritten history is equivalent to the secret never having existed
No — every clone, fork, or CI cache made before the rewrite still has the original history with the secret in it, untouched by the force-push
Yes, but only if branch protection is also disabled first
No, because force-pushing is blocked by git whenever secrets are present
items.explanation: History rewriting is good hygiene for the canonical repository going forward, but it only changes that one remote — it can't reach into copies that already exist on someone else's disk (a teammate's clone, a fork, a CI cache) made before the rewrite. Those copies still contain the original, unrewritten history. Rewriting history is not a substitute for rotation.
items.reference:
commit A: password added → commit B: password deleted
both commits still exist — B doesn't erase A, it adds on top of it

Why: "the file looks clean at HEAD" and "the repository is clean" are different claims — only scanning full history checks the second one.

items.prompt: A CI build step crashes and dumps its full environment to the build log for debugging purposes. The build log is retained for 60 days and is readable by anyone in the engineering org. What's the actual exposure window here?
choices: Zero — CI logs are only visible to the person who triggered the build
Up to 60 days, to everyone with log-viewer access in the org — not just the moment the crash happened
Exactly as long as the build takes to run
CI logs never contain real environment variable values, only variable names
items.explanation: Once the secret is written into the log, the exposure window is defined by the log's retention period and who can read it — often far broader and longer-lived than the few seconds the crash itself took. A secret 'only' printed once to a widely-readable, long-retained log is not a small or brief exposure.
items.reference:
echo $DB_PASSWORD in a debug step writes the real value into a log that's often more widely readable, and longer retained, than the source repo itself

Why: masking (see CI injection in L3) exists specifically to stop this exact print from ever showing the real value.

items.prompt: A CI platform automatically masks any value pulled from its own secret store, replacing it with `***` in log output — even for an accidental `echo $SECRET`. Does this mean CI-log leakage is a fully solved problem once masking is enabled?
choices: Yes — masking makes it impossible for a secret to ever appear in a log
No — masking only catches values the platform knows came from its secret store; a secret computed, transformed, or hardcoded outside that mechanism can still print unmasked
Yes, but only for the first 24 hours after the secret is created
No, masking only works for values shorter than 20 characters
items.explanation: Masking works by pattern-matching known secret values the platform itself injected — if a script derives a new string from the secret (e.g. base64-encodes it, or concatenates it into a longer string), or if a secret was hardcoded rather than pulled from the platform's store, the masking mechanism doesn't recognize it and it can print in full.
items.reference:
echo $DB_PASSWORD in a debug step writes the real value into a log that's often more widely readable, and longer retained, than the source repo itself

Why: masking (see CI injection in L3) exists specifically to stop this exact print from ever showing the real value.

items.prompt: In the inject → manage → rotate → scan pipeline, which step is the only one that runs BEFORE a secret is ever committed, rather than reacting to one that already exists somewhere?
choices: Rotation
Pre-commit scanning
Secret-manager storage
Env-var injection at runtime
items.explanation: Pre-commit scanning runs at the moment of committing, catching a secret-shaped string before it ever reaches a shared branch. Injection, secret-manager storage, and rotation all assume a secret already exists somewhere and manage it responsibly from there — scanning is the only step positioned to prevent the leak from happening at all.
items.reference:
Dev writes code → pre-commit scan → CI (masked inject) → secret manager → rotation schedule

Why: the four ideas run continuously as one pipeline, not as four independent tools checked off once.

items.prompt: A CI pipeline is set up to inject secrets from a secret manager as masked environment variables at build time. What has this step NOT yet addressed, that scanning would catch instead?
choices: Whether the CI logs will print the value unmasked
Whether a secret is already hardcoded somewhere in the source that CI checks out and runs
Whether the secret manager itself is reachable from the build agent
Nothing — injection alone makes hardcoded secrets in source irrelevant
items.explanation: Injecting secrets at build time solves how a running process gets its secrets — it does nothing to detect a secret someone already hardcoded directly into source, which CI will happily check out and run right alongside the injected ones. Scanning is a separate, earlier line of defense aimed specifically at that gap.
items.reference:
Dev writes code → pre-commit scan → CI (masked inject) → secret manager → rotation schedule

Why: the four ideas run continuously as one pipeline, not as four independent tools checked off once.

items.prompt: Once a leak is confirmed, which step in the pipeline is the one that actually ends the exposure — as opposed to investigating it or preventing the next one?
choices: Auditing access logs
Rotation
Adding a pre-commit scanner
Notifying affected users
items.explanation: Auditing logs tells you what already happened; adding a scanner prevents the next incident; notification is a separate obligation. Only rotation changes the value itself at the system that accepts it — which is the one action that makes the already-leaked copy stop working, ending the exposure rather than reacting to or preventing it.
items.reference:
Dev writes code → pre-commit scan → CI (masked inject) → secret manager → rotation schedule

Why: the four ideas run continuously as one pipeline, not as four independent tools checked off once.

items.prompt: A team stores secrets as plain `.env` files copied by hand onto each server, versus using a secret manager. What does the secret manager provide that scattered `.env` files structurally can't?
choices: Nothing meaningful — both approaches keep secrets out of source control equally well
An audit trail (who fetched which secret, and when) and one place to change a value that every consumer picks up automatically
Secret managers only add cost without any operational benefit
`.env` files are actually more secure because they never leave the server
items.explanation: Both approaches can keep a secret out of source control, but scattered `.env` files give no visibility into who accessed what and when, and rotating a value means manually updating every server that has a copy. A secret manager centralizes both: one audit trail, and one place to change a value that every consumer resolves fresh, without a manual per-server update.
items.reference:
Scattered .env files

no audit trail, manual update per server

Secret manager

one audit trail, one place to rotate

Why: a secret manager centralizes exactly the two things that make rotation and incident response fast.

items.prompt: After a suspected leak, a team using a secret manager rotates the value in one place and every service picks it up within minutes via its cache TTL. A team using hand-copied `.env` files has the equivalent task ahead of them. What does that second team actually have to do?
choices: Nothing extra — restarting the secret manager fixes both cases equally
Manually update the `.env` file on every server or environment that has a copy, and restart or redeploy each one
Wait for the next scheduled deploy, since `.env` files update themselves automatically
Delete the old `.env` files — deletion alone is equivalent to rotation
items.explanation: Without a central store, rotating a value means finding every place a copy was hand-placed and updating each one individually — a slower, more error-prone process exactly at the moment speed matters most (during incident response). This is the practical cost of the audit-trail/single-source-of-truth benefit a secret manager provides.
items.reference:
Scattered .env files

no audit trail, manual update per server

Secret manager

one audit trail, one place to rotate

Why: a secret manager centralizes exactly the two things that make rotation and incident response fast.

items.prompt: A frontend build script embeds an API secret into the compiled JavaScript bundle using an env-var-injection step, reasoning that injection is the recommended pattern. Why doesn't that reasoning hold here?
choices: It does hold — injection is injection, regardless of where the code runs
Injection only protects source control from holding the literal value — it says nothing about the fact that the compiled bundle, containing the resolved value, ships to every visitor's browser
The problem is only that the build script is slow, not that the value is exposed
Frontend bundles are never readable by end users, only by the build system
items.explanation: Injection solves 'don't commit the literal value to source' — it doesn't solve 'don't let the resolved value reach an untrusted environment.' A frontend bundle is compiled once and then served, as-is, to every visitor's browser; whatever value was resolved into it at build time is now public, no matter how cleanly it got there.
items.reference:
A value baked into client-side JS at build time ships to every visitor's browser — it was never actually secret, regardless of how it got there

Why: "injected, not hardcoded" protects source control, not the browser the code eventually runs in.

items.prompt: What's the correct fix for a frontend feature that genuinely needs to call a third-party API using a secret key?
choices: Obfuscate or minify the bundle so the key is harder to find
Route the call through your own backend, which holds the real secret server-side and the frontend only talks to your backend
Rotate the key more frequently so any given leak matters less
Store the key in `sessionStorage` instead of directly in the bundle
items.explanation: Obfuscation, faster rotation, and browser storage all still leave the real secret reachable from client-side code or the network requests it makes — none of them change the fact that untrusted code (running on someone else's machine) has the value. The only fix that actually keeps the secret secret is never sending it to the client at all: the frontend calls your backend, and your backend — which you control — holds and uses the real key.
items.reference:
A value baked into client-side JS at build time ships to every visitor's browser — it was never actually secret, regardless of how it got there

Why: "injected, not hardcoded" protects source control, not the browser the code eventually runs in.

items.prompt: A developer says 'it's fine, users would have to open dev tools and dig through the minified bundle to find it.' Is minification a meaningful protection here?
choices: Yes — minified code is effectively unreadable, so this is equivalent to real protection
No — minification changes variable names and formatting, not the actual string value, which is trivially searchable in the bundle's text
Yes, as long as source maps are also disabled in production
It depends on which minifier was used
items.explanation: Minification renames variables and strips whitespace — it does not encrypt or remove string literals. A secret value baked in as a string constant remains a plain, searchable string in the shipped bundle regardless of how unreadable the surrounding code structure looks; anyone can `Ctrl+F` the network tab or the downloaded file for it.
items.reference:
A value baked into client-side JS at build time ships to every visitor's browser — it was never actually secret, regardless of how it got there

Why: "injected, not hardcoded" protects source control, not the browser the code eventually runs in.

items.prompt: Implement `requireEnv(env, name)`, where `env` is a plain object simulating `process.env`. Return `env[name]` if it's set and non-empty; otherwise throw an `Error` (any message is fine, as long as it throws).

tests.description: returns the value when present
throws when the key is missing
throws when the key is present but empty

items.explanation: This is the fail-fast pattern from L3's `config/database.mjs`: a missing or empty required value throws immediately and loudly, rather than letting `undefined` silently flow into a connection string and fail later with a confusing, unrelated error message three requests in.
items.reference:
requireEnv(env, 'DB_HOST') → value or throws, at startup — not a silent undefined

Why: failing loudly at startup catches a missing secret in seconds; a silent undefined surfaces as a confusing bug much later.

items.prompt: Implement `loadConfig(env, requiredKeys)` where `env` is a plain object and `requiredKeys` is an array of strings. Return an object containing each key mapped to its value from `env`. If ANY key is missing or empty, throw an `Error` instead of returning a partial object.

tests.description: returns all values when every key is present
throws if any single required key is missing
throws if a required key is present but empty

items.explanation: This generalizes single-key `requireEnv` to a whole config object at once, matching L3's `dbConfig` shape (`DB_HOST`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD`, `DB_NAME` all required together) — the key property is still that a single missing value fails the whole load rather than returning a config object with a silent gap in it.
items.reference:
requireEnv(env, 'DB_HOST') → value or throws, at startup — not a silent undefined

Why: failing loudly at startup catches a missing secret in seconds; a silent undefined surfaces as a confusing bug much later.

items.prompt: Implement `missingKeys(env, requiredKeys)` that returns an array of every key in `requiredKeys` that is missing or empty in `env`, in the same order they appear in `requiredKeys`. Return an empty array if nothing is missing (this version reports gaps instead of throwing, useful for a startup health-check log).

tests.description: returns empty array when nothing is missing
reports one missing key
reports an empty-string value as missing too

items.explanation: A reporting variant of the same fail-fast idea: instead of throwing on the first gap, it collects every gap at once — useful for a startup health check that wants to tell an operator 'these three variables are all missing' in one message instead of one throw-fix-rerun cycle per variable.
items.reference:
requireEnv(env, 'DB_HOST') → value or throws, at startup — not a silent undefined

Why: failing loudly at startup catches a missing secret in seconds; a silent undefined surfaces as a confusing bug much later.

items.prompt: Implement `findAwsKeys(text)` that returns an array of every substring matching an AWS Access Key ID pattern (`AKIA` followed by exactly 16 uppercase letters/digits) found in `text`. Return an empty array if none are found.

tests.description: finds a single AWS key in a larger string
returns an empty array when there's no match
finds multiple matches in the same text

items.explanation: This is one of the five detectors from L3's `secret-scanner.mjs` in isolation — a pattern-matching detector that recognizes a known vendor's key format. It's real and useful, but it only catches values shaped exactly like this pattern; a differently-formatted secret (like Mira's plain `DB_PASSWORD` string) passes through completely undetected, which is exactly what L3's Checkpoint on this section explores.
items.reference:
/AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}/g

Why: pattern detectors catch known vendor key shapes reliably, but miss anything that doesn't match a known pattern — a real trade-off, not a bug to fix away.

items.prompt: Implement `hasPrivateKeyHeader(text)` that returns `true` if `text` contains a PEM private key header (`-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----`, `-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----`, or `-----BEGIN EC PRIVATE KEY-----`), and `false` otherwise.

tests.description: detects a plain PRIVATE KEY header
detects an RSA PRIVATE KEY header
returns false when there's no private key header

items.explanation: A private key's PEM header is one of the most reliable secret signatures to detect — unlike a plain password string, it has a fixed, unmistakable format that essentially never appears outside an actual key file, so this detector has a very low false-positive rate compared to something like a generic long-string heuristic.
items.reference:
/AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}/g

Why: pattern detectors catch known vendor key shapes reliably, but miss anything that doesn't match a known pattern — a real trade-off, not a bug to fix away.

items.prompt: Implement `findApiKeyAssignments(text)` that returns an array of every full matched substring shaped like `api_key = "..."`, `secret: '...'`, or `token="..."` (any of the words api_key/secret/token, case-insensitive, followed by `:` or `=`, then a quoted string of at least 8 characters). Return an empty array if none match.

tests.description: finds a double-quoted api_key assignment
finds a single-quoted secret assignment, case-insensitive
does not match a short quoted value under 8 chars

items.explanation: This is the 'generic assignment' detector from L3's scanner — it catches secrets that don't match any specific vendor's key format, by instead recognizing the shape of the code around them (a suspicious variable name assigned a long quoted string). It's broader than the AWS-key detector but also more prone to false positives on legitimately long non-secret strings, the trade-off L3's second Checkpoint discusses directly.
items.reference:
/AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}/g

Why: pattern detectors catch known vendor key shapes reliably, but miss anything that doesn't match a known pattern — a real trade-off, not a bug to fix away.

items.explanation: This is the mechanism behind CI's automatic masking of `secrets.*` values in log output (L3's GitHub Actions example): before a line is written to a log, every known secret substring is swapped out. `split`/`join` (rather than a regex) sidesteps needing to escape special regex characters that could appear in an arbitrary secret value.

Why: masking is a log-hygiene guard on values that are already accessible, not an access-control boundary.

items.prompt: Implement `maskPartial(secretValue)` that returns a partially-masked version of a secret suitable for a support ticket or log line: keep the first 2 and last 2 characters visible, replace everything in between with `'*'` repeated to match the original length. For strings 4 characters or shorter, return `'*'.repeat(secretValue.length)` (fully masked, too short to safely reveal any of it).

items.explanation: Full redaction (`***`) is right for logs, where the value should never be reconstructible. items.prompt: Implement `secretStillInHistory(commits, secret)` where `commits` is an array of commit diff strings (like `git log -p` output, one string per commit) and `secret` is the literal value being searched for. Return `true` if `secret` appears in ANY commit in the array, even if the most recent commit (the last element) doesn't contain it.

tests.description: finds a secret in an earlier commit even when the latest one is clean
tests.expr: expect(secretStillInHistory(["+ const x = 'SECRET123'", "- const x = 'SECRET123'\n+ const x = process.env.X"], 'SECRET123')).toBe(true)

tests.description: returns false when the secret never appears in any commit
returns true when only the most recent commit contains it

items.explanation: This is the toy version of L3's `git log -p --all | grep` transcript: checking the CURRENT file (equivalent to checking only the last commit) is exactly the check that reports 'clean' while the secret is still fully present earlier in the array — which is why a real audit has to check every commit, not just HEAD.
items.reference:
grep -c SECRET config.js → 0 (clean at HEAD)
git log -p --all | grep SECRET → found (still in history)

Why: "the current file is clean" and "the repository is clean" are different claims, and only the second one matters for exposure.

items.prompt: Implement `isRotationOverdue(daysSinceLastRotation, maxAgeDays)`. Return `true` if `daysSinceLastRotation` is greater than or equal to `maxAgeDays`, `false` otherwise.

tests.description: overdue when past the max age
not overdue when well within the max age
counts exactly hitting the max age as overdue

items.explanation: This is the check behind L2's scheduled-rotation idea: a secret's maximum useful age bounds how long ANY leak of it (caught or not) stays valid. A monitoring job running this check across every stored secret is how 'we rotate every 90 days' becomes something that actually happens, rather than a policy nobody enforces.
items.reference:
Scheduled rotation bounds how long any leak (caught or not) stays valid — it doesn't replace scanning for secrets that were never in the rotation system at all

Why: "scheduled rotation is on" and "this specific secret is actually covered by it" are different claims — an old, un-migrated service can be outside the schedule entirely.
